opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the starting point was a pretty simple observation. When GPT-3 came out, it showed that scaling up dense models gives you remarkable capabilities, but it also showed how expensive that path is. Every single token you process has to go through every single parameter in the network. That felt wasteful to us, because intuitively not every piece of knowledge the model has is relevant to every input. If you're processing a sentence about chemistry, you probably don't need the parts of the model that are really good at, say, translating poetry.

Mixture-of-experts addresses that directly. You can grow the total capacity of the model enormously, adding many more parameters and much more room to store knowledge, while each token only gets routed to a small subset of experts. So the compute per token stays relatively modest even as the model gets much bigger. That decoupling of model capacity from compute cost was the key thing that made it exciting.

There was also a lot of groundwork at Google already. Noam Shazeer and others had done the early sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts work, and then GShard and Switch Transformer showed that you could actually train these things at scale on TPUs. So it wasn't a shot in the dark. We had reasons to believe the infrastructure and the routing techniques were mature enough.

With GLaM, the bet was: can we build something with far more total parameters than GPT-3, over a trillion, but where each token only activates a fraction of that, and end up with better quality while using significantly less energy to train and less compute at inference? And that's what we found. We got better zero-shot and few-shot performance across a broad set of tasks while using roughly a third of the training energy.

Part of what made it compelling to me personally is the efficiency argument. If these models are going to be used everywhere, the cost of training and serving them really matters, both financially and environmentally. Sparsity seemed like one of the most promising ways to keep scaling without the costs scaling the same way.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it came from a fairly simple observation about how compute was being spent. When GPT-3 came out, it was clear that scaling worked, but the way it scaled was that every single token had to go through every single parameter. So if you wanted a model with ten times the capacity, you paid ten times the compute for every token, whether that token needed it or not. And that felt wasteful to me, because intuitively most tokens don't need the whole model. If you're processing a bit of Python code, the parts of the network that are good at, say, French poetry probably aren't contributing much.

Mixture-of-experts gives you a way around that. You can have a very large number of parameters, but for any given token you only activate a small fraction of them. The router decides which experts to use, so you get the capacity of a huge model with the per-token cost of a much smaller one. That decoupling of parameter count from compute is really the whole story.

And the thing that made me optimistic, rather than just curious, was that Noam Shazeer and others at Google had already shown this working at reasonable scale a few years earlier. The pieces existed. What hadn't been done was taking that idea and pushing it to the frontier, to a regime where you're actually competing with the best dense models. So I saw it less as a bet on a new idea and more as a bet that an idea with known mechanics would hold up when scaled, and that the efficiency gains would let us go further than a dense model at the same training budget. That's essentially what GLaM was trying to demonstrate: that you could match or beat GPT-3 on quality while using a fraction of the energy and compute at inference time.

r001.rationale: It says MoE activates only a small fraction of parameters per token and that GLaM used a fraction of the energy and compute at inference.

astra-6.text:
The appeal was that you could increase a model’s capacity without increasing the computation for every token by the same amount. In a dense model, all the parameters participate in processing each token. With a mixture-of-experts model, you have different expert networks, and a router selects a small number of them for each token.

That gives you a way to build a much larger model while keeping the cost of training and running it more manageable. If the goal is to get beyond GPT-3, that’s an attractive direction: can we give the model more capacity to learn without paying the full computational cost of a much larger dense model?

Of course, having more parameters doesn’t automatically make it better. You still have to get the routing right and make sure the experts are being used effectively. But that separation between total capacity and computation per token was the central promise.

sol-6.1.text:
What appealed to us was the ability to increase the model’s capacity without increasing the computation for every token by the same amount. In a dense model like GPT-3, you use essentially all the parameters for every token. With mixture-of-experts, a router selects a small subset of experts, so you can have a much larger total number of parameters while keeping the computation per token relatively manageable.

That gave us a promising way to explore whether more capacity could translate into better quality at a practical training cost. Of course, it wasn’t automatic—you still had to make the routing work, balance the load across experts, and train the whole system reliably. But it offered another dimension for scaling beyond simply making a dense model bigger.
